questions.prompt: The toy uses 16-byte pages; page 1 maps to frame 7. Where does a permitted read at virtual 21 translate?

options.label: With 16-byte pages, virtual 21 has page 1 and offset 5; frame 7 gives physical 117.
Physical 21, because virtual and physical addresses must match.
Physical 112, because translation removes the offset.

questions.explanation: Integer division gives page 1 and remainder 5. Replace the page number with frame 7 while retaining the offset: 7*16+5=117. These sizes belong to the fictional fixture.

questions.prompt: Page 1 is read-only and page 2 has no present mapping. What must happen before a target access?

options.label: Translate and write first, then report a protection failure.
Use physical address zero whenever a mapping is absent.
Check mapping presence and permission before translating or accessing the target.

questions.explanation: A permitted read, forbidden write and missing mapping are distinct cases. Check presence and operation permission first; rejection performs no target access and this toy does not implement fault recovery.

questions.prompt: An upward-growing segment has base 100 and exclusive length 12. Which boundary is correct?

options.label: Offset 11 translates to 11 because the base is ignored.
For base 100 and exclusive limit 12, offset 11 maps to 111; offset 12 is rejected.
Offset 12 is valid because the length is inclusive.

questions.explanation: The accepted logical range is 0 through 11. Check offset < 12 and permission before adding base 100. A different segment representation needs its own bound and growth-direction contract.

questions.prompt: An 18-byte allocation uses two 16-byte pages; separate variable-sized free holes are 6 and 6. What do these examples show?

options.label: Paging can waste space inside a final page; variable segments can leave separated free holes.
The unused page tail and separate holes are identical allocation failures.
A contiguous 10-byte segment always fits because total free memory is 12.

questions.explanation: The page allocation leaves 14 bytes inside its last fixed unit. Separated six-byte holes cannot supply one contiguous ten-byte segment under the stated policy; internal and external waste differ.

questions.prompt: A review proposes ordinary pointer writes and memcpy for portable device-register access. What is the appropriate contract?

options.label: Every mapped address behaves exactly like normal RAM.
A CPU store proves that a posted device write has completed.
Use the documented platform device-I/O accessors and ordering rules; an ordinary pointer is not a portable MMIO contract.

questions.explanation: Platform mapping tokens, accessors and ordering/posting rules define portable device I/O. Ordinary RAM operations do not replace that contract; a device-specific completion rule may still be needed.
